newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania minister may quit over oil restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Romania minister may quit over oil restructuring.

text.p: Romania's Trade and Industry minister has threatened to resign unless plans are quickly implemented to slim down the country's bloated oil industry, including the creation of a national oil company.
"Plans for the future company have been in preparation for more than two months but they haven't taken shape," Calin Popescu Tariceanu said on television late on Thursday.
"I am very concerned about this. I have no intention of resigning now but I'm prepared to do so if I cannot push through my plans."

The centrist government was to meet on Friday to consider revisions to the 1997 budget, a key provision for securing further credits from international lenders. An International Monetary Fund mission is in Bucharest examining Romania's success in implementing reforms.
Tariceanu said Romania's 11 refineries with an annual capacity of 33 million tonnes had to be reduced to the level of domestic consumption of about 10 million tonnes.
"The IMF does not want to see unviable oil companies operating at a loss," he said. "We must take decisions on what we want to do."

The centrist government, committed to fostering reforms stalled during seven years of leftist rule, has pledged set up a firm to replace the National Oil Comapny (CRP) holding to streamline the oil sector and assure smooth cash flow.
The CRP was initially supposed to cease activity on August 1 but no structure has been set up to replace it.
The new company was planned to group three refineries, but the World Bank has opposed the proposal, saying one facility, Arpechim near Pitesti, 110 (70 miles) north of Bucharest, was sufficient.
Romanian officials say the country's pipeline network is inadequate to get supplies to a single refinery and Tariceanu said he wanted at least two to stay under the state umbrella.

The State Ownership Fund was to have announced on Friday plans to privatise another refinery, Petromidia on the Black Sea coast, but postponed the decision for a week, saying documentation was insufficent. Seven firms have submitted bids.

Petromidia is among 12 major loss-making enterprises which had originally been earmarked for closure under government reform plans after a history of failing to secure constant crude oil supplies. But it attracts considerable from investors in Romania's budding capital market.
